documents.title: AI Use Syllabus Statements
documents.stance_why: The page says including an AI syllabus statement "is at the discretion of each instructor" and offers sample statements at three named levels ("Prohibited", "Assisted", "Integrated") ranging from a full ban to required use. It sets no single rule itself, so it delegates and lists the tiers.
tiers: Level 3: Integrated (AI Tools Encouraged and Fully Allowed)
documents.summary: Provost-hosted guidance with general recommendations (be clear, define terms, mind equity, point to support services) and sample syllabus statements at three levels of AI permission. Instructors choose whether and which to use. The samples stress citation and prompt documentation, verifying output, and treating undisclosed or prohibited use as an integrity violation.

units.why: The statement says the samples help professors build their own policies and that including one is "at the discretion of each instructor", so the university hands the decision to instructors (P04), not a syllabus mandate (P09).
units.anchor: is at the discretion of each instructor
units.policy: Using or including an AI-related syllabus statement is at the discretion of each instructor.

units.why: The overview frames AI as having "positive, negative, and neutral" impact and sets the purpose of the guidance; this is a preamble of principle, so P56 and modality informs.
units.anchor: recognizes the prevalence of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and services

units.why: The sample statements exist "to assist professors in developing the appropriate policies or guidance for student use of AI tools", a purpose and scope statement for the guidance, so P56 rather than P04, which is about who decides.
units.anchor: intended to assist professors in developing the appropriate policies or guidance

units.why: The recommendation to name "the category of tool" rather than products is advice on wording a syllabus rule so it covers all tools, which fits P61 (defining coverage) only partly, so the fit_note records the wording advice.
units.anchor: rather than specific products, e.g., ChatGPT
units.policy: Syllabus statements should reference the category of tool or service, such as "Generative AI tools", rather than specific products, since multiple tools and services are available.
units.fit_note: P61 is about defining AI and scope; this unit advises wording rules by tool category instead of by product name, not a definition.

units.why: "Be clear in what is allowed or prohibited, and any conditions" tells instructors to state expectations explicitly, which is P09 (state AI expectations in the syllabus) with modality should.
units.anchor: Be clear in what is allowed or prohibited, and any conditions
units.policy: Instructors should be clear about what is allowed or prohibited and any conditions, such as citations, limitations in scope, or limitations by specific product.

units.why: "Provide definitions to promote understanding and support expectations" asks syllabus authors to define terms, matching P61 (define AI and scope).
units.anchor: Provide definitions to promote understanding and support expectations.

units.why: "Be mindful of equity ... economic hardships for fee-based tools" is an equity and access recommendation, so P51.
units.anchor: Establish a level playing field for all students
units.policy: Instructors should be mindful of equity, establish a level playing field for all students, and be mindful of any economic hardships for fee-based tools or services.

units.why: Instructors are told to "direct students to ... library services, writing centers, tutoring" so students have human help; P72 fits, with a fit_note because the unit also points to integrity policies.
units.anchor: library services, writing centers, tutoring opportunities, or other academic support resources
units.policy: Instructors should direct students to the school's academic integrity or academic dishonesty policies, as well as library services, writing centers, tutoring opportunities, or other academic support resources.
units.fit_note: Also directs students to integrity policies, which P72 (human help) does not cover.

units.why: The page sorts sample statements into named levels ("Prohibited", "Assisted", "Integrated"), which is an explicit tier scheme, so P05; the document itself sets no single stance.
units.anchor: Level 2: Assisted (AI Tools Partially Allowed)

units.why: Example 1 bases the ban on learning outcomes ("writing, analytical, and critical thinking skills are part of the learning outcomes"), which explains that doing the work builds skill, so P41.
units.anchor: writing, analytical, and critical thinking skills are part of the learning outcomes

units.why: "AI-generated submissions are not permitted" bars students from submitting AI-produced work, so P19 with must-not and prohibit.
units.anchor: AI-generated submissions are not permitted

units.why: "will be treated as plagiarism" classifies AI-generated submissions as misconduct, so P36 (not P19, which is the ban itself).
units.anchor: will be treated as plagiarism

units.why: Example 2 states generative AI "is not permitted in any aspect of this class", a blanket course-wide ban, so P01.
units.anchor: not permitted in any aspect of this class
units.policy: The use of generative AI, AI writing, or similar AI tools or services is not permitted in any aspect of this class.

units.why: "considered a violation of academic integrity and be reported accordingly" makes AI use misconduct handled by the integrity process, so P36.
units.anchor: considered a violation of academic integrity and be reported accordingly

units.why: Example 3 gives careers and learning outcomes as reasons ("critical to the learning outcomes of this class and to preparing you for future careers"), a rationale for doing the work yourself, so P41.
units.anchor: critical to the learning outcomes of this class and to preparing you for future careers

units.why: "complete all work themselves without ... assistance from anyone or anything, including artificial intelligence" bans all AI help and outside help; P01 (default ban) fits better than P19 because it bars any assistance, not just generation.
units.anchor: complete all work themselves without outside collaboration or assistance from anyone or anything
units.policy: Students are expected to complete all work themselves without outside collaboration or assistance from anyone or anything, including artificial intelligence (AI) tools and services.

units.why: "unauthorized tools, services, and sources will be treated as plagiarism" classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct, so P36.
units.anchor: unauthorized tools, services, and sources will be treated as plagiarism

units.why: "Produce your own work" is a short expectation that students own what they submit, so P29.
units.anchor: Produce your own work.

units.why: "Verify your sources and facts" tells students to check what they use; it is listed among expectations of this no-AI statement, so P31 (verify output) fits partly and the fit_note says it concerns sources generally.
units.anchor: Verify your sources and facts.
units.fit_note: Does not mention AI output; it asks students to verify sources and facts in general.

units.why: Example 4 allows "University library research databases and word processor spelling and grammar checkers" while barring writing tools; permitting grammar checkers is a prose-tool rule, so P18 with permit.
units.anchor: word processor spelling and grammar checkers
units.policy: Some technologies are allowed, such as University library research databases and word processor spelling and grammar checkers.
units.fit_note: P18 is about AI for prose; here the permitted tools are non-AI spelling and grammar checkers listed as exceptions to a ban.

units.why: "the use of writing tools or services (AI-based, human, or combinations thereof) is not permitted" bans AI and human writing help for this work, so P19 with must-not.
units.anchor: the use of writing tools or services (AI-based, human, or combinations thereof) is not permitted
units.policy: The use of writing tools or services (AI-based, human, or combinations thereof) is not permitted.

units.why: The same sentence says such use "will be considered a violation of academic integrity", an integrity classification separate from the ban, so P36.
units.anchor: will be considered a violation of academic integrity

units.why: "an AI tool ... cannot be considered a member of the group" treats AI as an outside party under group-work rules, so P45 (AI like a human collaborator under existing rules).
units.anchor: an AI tool or any outside person, organization, or other service
units.policy: In group assignments, an AI tool or any outside person, organization, or other service, system, source, or entity cannot be considered a member of the group.

units.why: Example 1 justifies AI use as preparation for work ("co-pilot" mode will become a component of future work), so P44.
units.anchor: working with Generative AI in a “co-pilot” mode will become a component of future work

units.why: AI "may be used as part of the curriculum when approved by the School/instructor" makes AI use conditional on approval, a restrict position decided by the school or instructor, so P04.
units.anchor: may be used as part of the curriculum when approved by the School/instructor
units.policy: Generative AI tools may be used as part of the curriculum when approved by the School/instructor.

units.why: "Students must review and modify the Generative AI output as appropriate" requires critical handling of AI output; P31 fits partly, so the fit_note says it is about modifying output, not only checking accuracy.
units.anchor: Students must review and modify the Generative AI output as appropriate
units.policy: Students must review and modify the Generative AI output as appropriate.
units.fit_note: Requires review and modification of AI output, not specifically checking it for errors.

units.why: "your work will be assessed on the value you add to the initial output" ties grading to the student contribution beyond the AI output, a grading design around AI, so P35.
units.anchor: your work will be assessed on the value you add to the initial output

units.why: "You must include both the raw Generative AI output and your value-added final product" requires submitting the AI output with the work; P26 (submit logs/transcripts) fits partly, so the fit_note names the raw-output requirement.
units.anchor: You must include both the “raw” Generative AI output and your value-added final product
units.policy: Students must include both the "raw" Generative AI output and their value-added final product in the assignment submission.
units.fit_note: Requires the raw AI output itself rather than a transcript, log, or reflection.

units.why: Example 2 states "Generative AI as a translation and grammar checking tool is permitted", a prose-specific permission, so P18.
units.anchor: Generative AI as a translation and grammar checking tool is permitted
units.policy: The use of Generative AI as a translation and grammar checking tool is permitted in this course.

units.why: "Generative AI tools may not always provide accurate translations or catch all grammar errors" warns that output is imperfect, so P31.
units.anchor: may not always provide accurate translations or catch all grammar errors

units.why: "consult with instructors or language resources" points students to human help beside the AI tool, so P72.
units.anchor: consult with instructors or language resources for comprehensive feedback and guidance

units.why: Example 1: "You may use AI programs ... to help generate ideas and brainstorm" is a brainstorming permission, so P15.
units.anchor: You may use AI programs (e.g., ChatGPT) to help generate ideas and brainstorm.

units.why: "it should be cited like any other reference material" requires acknowledging AI use in the assignment, so P24.
units.anchor: it should be cited like any other reference material

units.why: "material generated by AI programs may be inaccurate, incomplete, or otherwise problematic" warns output can be wrong, so P31.
units.anchor: may be inaccurate, incomplete, or otherwise problematic

units.why: "use may also stifle your own independent thinking and creativity" warns AI can replace the student's thinking; P32 fits partly because it is a caution, not an instruction.
units.anchor: use may also stifle your own independent thinking and creativity
units.fit_note: A warning about the risk to independent thinking rather than an instruction to remain the primary problem-solver.

units.why: Example 2 compares AI to calculators, "incredible assistants", and welcomes use for "idea generation, synthesis, and information gathering"; P15 fits partly because the uses also include synthesis and gathering, noted in fit_note.
units.anchor: employing them for idea generation, synthesis, and information gathering
units.policy: Using AI tools effectively involves employing them for idea generation, synthesis, and information gathering to gain a comprehensive understanding of various topics.
units.fit_note: Also covers synthesis and information gathering, not only brainstorming.

units.why: "we, as users, take charge of guiding, verifying, and refining the ultimate answers" makes the student responsible for checking and shaping the output, so P31.
units.anchor: take charge of guiding, verifying, and refining the ultimate answers

units.why: "Simply copying and pasting without comprehension is ill-advised" discourages pasting output the student does not understand, so P30 (understand what you submit) with fit_note, modality should-not.
units.anchor: Simply copying and pasting without comprehension is ill-advised.
units.fit_note: Gives advice against pasting without comprehension; does not require students to be able to explain every line.

units.why: Example 2 repeats the citation rule in its own wording ("cited like any other reference material"), with a note on reference quality; coded as P24 because each example is its own statement.
units.anchor: it should be cited like any other reference material (with due consideration

units.why: Example 3: "I expect you to use Generative AI tools in this class. In fact, some assignments will require it." expects and requires AI use, so P02 with require.
units.anchor: some assignments will require it

units.why: "Learning to use AI is an emerging skill that will be useful in a competitive workplace" gives the career rationale, so P44.
units.anchor: Learning to use AI is an emerging skill that will be useful

units.why: "If you provide minimum effort prompts, you will get low-quality results" teaches prompt craft; no type covers advice about prompt quality, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: You will need to refine your prompts to achieve good outcomes.
units.uncovered_note: Students should refine their prompts, because low-effort prompts give low-quality results (advice on prompting skill).

units.why: "Don't trust anything it says ... assume it is wrong unless you ... can check it with another source" tells students to verify AI output, so P31.
units.anchor: assume it is wrong unless you either know the answer or can

units.why: "You will be responsible for any errors or omissions provided by the tool" makes students answerable for AI mistakes in their work, so P29.
units.anchor: You will be responsible for any errors or omissions provided by the tool.

units.why: "include a paragraph at the end of any assignment ... explaining what you used the AI for and what prompts you used" requires a statement with tool use and prompts, so P25 (details such as prompts) rather than P24.
units.anchor: include a paragraph at the end of any assignment that uses AI
units.policy: Students include a paragraph at the end of any assignment that uses AI explaining what they used the AI for and what prompts they used to get the results.

units.why: "Failure to do so is in violation of the academic honesty policies" makes non-disclosure itself the violation, so P28.
units.anchor: Failure to do so is in violation of the academic honesty policies.

units.why: Example 4: "Using an AI content generator ... without proper attribution violates academic integrity" makes missing attribution the violation, so P28.
units.anchor: without proper attribution violates academic integrity

units.why: "you pledge to affirm that they are your own work and that you attribute the use of any tools and sources" is a student pledge of ownership and attribution; P29 chosen since it is about owning submissions.
units.anchor: you pledge to affirm that they are your own work
units.policy: By submitting assignments, students pledge to affirm that they are their own work and that they attribute the use of any tools and sources.
units.fit_note: Combines ownership of work with a pledge to attribute tools and sources.

units.why: "Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is an important skill in today’s society" is a professional-skill rationale, so P44.
units.anchor: Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is an important skill

units.why: "Master prompt engineering by refining your prompts" repeats the prompt-craft advice in Example 4; no type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Master “prompt engineering” by refining your prompts in order to get good outcomes.
units.uncovered_note: Students should master prompt engineering by refining prompts to get good outcomes (advice on prompting skill).

units.why: "Fact-check all of the AI outputs. Assume it is wrong unless you cross-check" requires verification, so P31.
units.anchor: Fact-check all of the AI outputs.

units.why: "You will be responsible for any errors or omissions" in Example 4 puts responsibility for AI errors on the student, so P29.
units.anchor: You will be responsible for any errors or omissions.

units.why: "the use of AI should be acknowledged ... write a short paragraph to explain which AI tool and how you used it ... Include the prompts" requires tool and prompt details, so P25.
units.anchor: write a short paragraph to explain which AI tool and how you used it
units.policy: At the end of the assignment, students write a short paragraph explaining which AI tool they used and how, and include the prompts they used to get the results.

units.why: "Failure to do so is in violation of academic integrity policies" makes non-disclosure the violation in Example 4, so P28.
units.anchor: Failure to do so is in violation of academic integrity policies.

units.why: Example 5: "you will be expected to research, learn, and use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools" expects AI use in class activities, so P02 with require.
units.anchor: you will be expected to research, learn, and use generative artificial intelligence

units.why: "you will be held responsible for ensuring the accuracy and veracity of the content you will produce" makes students responsible for output accuracy; P31 fits (verify output) with a fit_note that responsibility is the point.
units.anchor: held responsible for ensuring the accuracy and veracity of the content you will produce
units.fit_note: Frames verification as responsibility for accuracy of submitted content.

units.why: "you must cite your use of AI-based tools within each submission" is a per-submission disclosure rule, so P24.
units.anchor: you must cite your use of AI-based tools within each submission

units.why: "separately document and attach your prompts, dialogue, and iterations with the AI for each assignment" requires submitting a log of the interaction, so P26.
units.anchor: separately document and attach your prompts, dialogue, and iterations with the AI

units.why: The resource guide is described as "a product of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Advisory Committee, formed and tasked by Provost Jay Brewster" to address AI in teaching, which records who made the guidance and why, so P56 (informs).
units.anchor: formed and tasked by Provost Jay Brewster to address the impact and adoption of AI

notes: Only the provost sample-statement page was coded. The linked Academic Policy on Artificial Intelligence was not in the collected set. Two UNCOVERED units concern advice on prompting skill; a candidate type for prompt-craft guidance.
